nodes.name: Tabonuco
nodes.desc: Dominant tree of the lower tabonuco forest zone at El Yunque. Its trunk cavities can serve as nest sites for the Puerto Rican parrot.

nodes.name: Pumpwood (yagrumo)
nodes.desc: A fast-growing pioneer tree that recolonizes hurricane-damaged ground. Birds and bats eat its fruit and spread the seeds.

nodes.name: Sierra palm
nodes.desc: Dominates the palm forest zone on shallow soils at about 600 m. Its fruit is eaten by birds in the forest.

nodes.name: Lira vine
nodes.desc: A climbing vine whose fruit and nectar are recorded in the diet of several forest birds.

nodes.name: Forest insects
nodes.desc: Leaf-eating and litter-dwelling insects. A coqui study at El Yunque linked frog presence to fewer flying insects and far less leaf damage.

nodes.name: Bananaquit
nodes.desc: Small, very commonly recorded bird that takes nectar and fruit. GloBI records it eating fruit of several forest plants.

nodes.name: Scaly-naped pigeon
nodes.desc: A fruit-eating pigeon, with GloBI records of it eating pumpwood, lira vine and sierra palm fruit.

nodes.name: Jamaican fruit bat
nodes.desc: A fruit-eating bat recorded feeding on pumpwood. Fruit-eating bats help spread forest seeds.

nodes.name: Puerto Rican parrot
nodes.desc: Critically endangered. Eats flowers, fruit, leaves and bark, and nests in tree cavities, favouring palo colorado trees. Hurricanes have repeatedly cut its numbers.

nodes.name: Black rat
nodes.desc: An introduced omnivore that eats parrot eggs and chicks. It is in turn prey for the Puerto Rican boa.

nodes.name: Common coquí
nodes.desc: A nocturnal sit-and-wait frog that mainly eats arthropods and can reach very high densities. It lays eggs on land and has no tadpole stage.

nodes.name: Gundlach's anole
nodes.desc: A common forest anole that eats small invertebrates. Young Puerto Rican boas feed mainly on anoles.

nodes.name: Puerto Rican tody
nodes.desc: A tiny insect-eating bird endemic to the island. GloBI also records it taking fruit of pumpwood.

nodes.name: Pearly-eyed thrasher
nodes.desc: An opportunistic omnivore that eats insects, fruit, lizards and frogs, and the eggs and nestlings of other birds. It competes with parrots for nest cavities.

nodes.name: Puerto Rican woodpecker
nodes.desc: An endemic woodpecker. GloBI records it eating fruit and the lizard Anolis krugi.

nodes.name: Small Indian mongoose
nodes.desc: An introduced predator that eats parrot eggs and chicks, and opportunistically takes coquís, according to the species accounts.

nodes.name: Puerto Rican boa
nodes.desc: The island's largest snake. Adults eat mostly mammals (rats and bats), plus birds, anoles and a few frogs.

nodes.name: Puerto Rican broad-winged hawk
nodes.desc: A rare forest hawk found in El Yunque's tabonuco forest. Raptors including hawks are listed among natural predators of the parrot.

nodes.name: Rainfall and cloud
nodes.desc: Trade winds rise over the mountains and drop heavy rain, in places over six metres a year, with no distinct dry season.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Warm, steady temperatures and light year-round drive growth, though cloud cover is frequent.

nodes.name: Hurricane winds
nodes.desc: Hugo, Georges, Irma and Maria damaged the forest and cut parrot numbers. Open gaps let pioneer trees such as pumpwood take over.

nodes.name: Soil nutrients
nodes.desc: Shallow, acidic soils in the higher forest zones; nutrients come mainly from recycled leaf litter.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, bacteria and litter invertebrates break down fallen leaves and wood and return nutrients to the soil.
